newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Fuel oil under pressure.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Fuel oil under pressure.

text.p: The fuel oil market is expected to shed some of its recent gains despite strong support from a large local trading firm as a deluge of arbitrage cargoes on top of an already well stocked Singapore weigh in heavily on prices.
The 180-centistoke grade fuel oil traded $102.5 per tonne on Friday, $1.50 off its intra-week traded high of $104 on Thursday but still higher than the $99.00 deal on Monday.
All cargoes were bought by the same trader who was attempting to repeat in the fuel market, his successful gas oil strategy where prices have soared by almost $3.00 per barrel in about three weeks.
But fuel oil traders say a combination of high stocks and large arbitrage cargoes might frustrate the trader's ambition as was the case late last week when deals were done off the week's high.
Residual fuel stocks in Singapore for the week ending March 19 rose by 932,000-tonnes to 11.76 million barrels after a 2.1-million build in the previous week.
"Suppliers held their cargoes last week, awaiting further price hikes by the local buyer," said one trader.
"But since stocks here are high and arbitrage cargoes are coming this way, prices will be under pressure," he said.
Some 250,000 tonnes of arbitrage cargoes have been coming from the Mediterranean to Asia, mainly to Singapore, since the beginning of March, traders said.
Many traders were skeptical about last week's rise, with some calling it a "pricing game."

In the gas oil market, traders expected the same local trader, who has bought nearly four million barrels in the past three weeks for end March/April lifting free-on board (fob) Singapore to remain active this week.

The trader's aim of keeping prices high is now aided by the large award by Indian Oil Corp (IOC) for May delivery cargoes. IOC bought a total of 870,000 tonnes in 21 cargoes exceeding even the most bullish predictions on Friday.
The Singapore trader, aiming at China's refinery maintenance season in March, remained active at the end of last week but some traders voiced concernes over the three-week-long buying.

"He is a brave man to be able to buy at such high levels as far as the endusers are able to pay at such levels," one trader said. "If he failed to place those cargoes into Indonesia or China, he will find a hard time to place them elsewhere."
China's Maoming Petrochemical Company will shutdown a 16,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) hydrocracker in end March for a month.
The 75,000-bpd crude unit of the Zhenhai Refinery and the 51,100-bpd Fujian refinery will also be shut down in April for maintenance.

On the physical market, a Japanese trader bought on 450,000 barrels on Friday ranging between $27.50 and $28.75 a barrel free-on-board (fob) basis for early to second-half April lifting after 760,000 barrels were traded a day earlier.
Demand is also boosted by Indonesia's demand for April at a projected 3.5 million to 4.0 million barrels.

Despite the active demand, at least 800,000 tonnes of Russian and Middle East cargoes are due to arrive Singapore soon, triggering concerns that prices might fall when the cargoes arrive, traders said.
In the naphtha market on Friday, April swaps fell 50 cents per barrel overnight to $23.30/$23.50 as buyers disappeared, traders said.
"There are alot of offers but no buyers in the East...naphtha is weakening," said one trader with a major oil company. "Most April requirements have already been covered."
The gasoline-naphtha spread, which had dipped as low as $3.20 earlier this week, found relief from the weaker naphtha and firmer gasoline.
"It should hit $4.00 soon if naphtha keeps falling," a trader said.
Gasoline found support despite a U.S. major aggressively offering fob Singapore cargoes.
